title: Rethinking Data: Moving From the Traditional Three-Tier Web Stack to Client-Side Event Sourcing

segments.text: Hello everybody. I am Olimpu Pop and
InfoQ editor
and I have the pleasure of discussing
today with Johannes Schickling
and he's one of the people involved with
local first movement conference and
comparing to the other discussions I had
with Martin Kletzmann and Adam Wiggins
today we'll go all in and understand
what's the difference of the mindset
that you have to shift from before
having local first in auto merge and
what changed with Johannes after he had
that. But without any further ado,
Johannes, please introduce yourself.
>> Hi, I'm Johannes Schickling. I live here
in wonderful Berlin. I'm originally also
from Germany, just moved a little bit
further north. I in the past am the
founder of Prisma, which was all about
server side database tooling and since
2020 I've taken a step away from Prisma
and been more exploring software and the
the future of software by myself and in
2020 I went all in on local first, which
are ideas by the the friends of mine at
Ink & Switch and been happily exploring
since and now combine those ideas of
local first with all the tailwinds we
got from AI.
>> Great.
As we discussed before
Prisma got quite important or I don't
know how to put it. People use it in the
JavaScript / TypeScript ecosystem.
So, how did you get started with it?
What were the challenges if you look
back, what would be the
aha moments that you had while getting
started?
>> Yeah, I mean, looking back at like me
now spending probably somewhere around
20 years with computers productively,
there's always like a a common theme of
like me trying to build something and
then me kind of getting frustrated with
the tools I have to build it. Like even
before computers, like I always wanted
to build something and then I kind of
got sidetracked and like rather build my
own tools that I can use to build
whatever I want to do.
And this is kind of like the recurring
pattern. Prisma was just like one
instance of that where like a decade
before I was just very frustrated with
like the database and API tooling, etc.
always being the bottleneck to build
anything.
In the past, I've used a lot of like
PHP, etc. and there there's like a
popular framework called Laravel, which
is still pretty big today. And this is
where I saw like how good database
tooling could be, also with Ruby on
Rails. But then using JavaScript mostly
and then TypeScript also emerging, there
was like nothing really comparable that
was meeting my goals and my hopes what
how good this could be. And particularly
the emergence with TypeScript felt like
the right moment to take another step,
go all in on database tooling that
embraces type safety with the goal of
just having better tooling to build
better applications. And I think that's
like still the true part today, that you
need to create tools to build great
applications.
But compared to Prisma, these days I'm
also rethinking the architecture quite a
lot where Prisma was all about like that
traditional architecture, like typically
like a three-tier web stack where
you have a like a centralized database
somewhere where you have an API tier,
maybe have like a a client tier. But I
wanted to think through a bit more like
how can we actually unlock the best
possible user experience? What sets the
highest bar? I think it's mostly like
desktop software, maybe very well-built
mobile software where whenever you like
click on something, something
immediately happens. Ideally, the
software works like no matter where you
are, whether you're on a plane. Think,
for example, an app like Apple Notes.
That works just super reliably under any
circumstances. But, you can't quite say
the same thing for like your average web
app.
And I wanted to flip that and
understand, like, hey, what is the
problem? Why can't we have the same
excellent experience with the most
dominant platform we have today, which
is the web? And I got the insights into
the direction to pursue through Ink &
Switch, my friends there, which then
have written that excellent local-first
paper or essay. And this was as
important to me that I kind of shifted
my my main focus to pursue this topic.
>> Okay, so you adhere to the ideals
because
that's how the other
members of the local-first saw it as a
couple of ideals and try to do things
properly. I'm thinking about the
discussion that I had with Adam Wiggins.
And what he's saying is that, well, he's
known for putting together Heroku, which
has cloud written all over it.
And then now it seems that it's the
polar opposite. But, what we agreed upon
is that
it was this this movement. People were
used to having things on their local
machines. They got to the cloud and then
they didn't have the same experience, so
something was missing. And local-first
is that sweet spot for each and every
one of us when we're building something
that allows you to have the same ideal
experience, utopian if you want, but
with the benefits of having the ability
of having distributed and not losing
data if something happens to the copy on
your machine.
>> It's hard to think about this in terms
of a spectrum. I think it's rather the
kind of very radical exploration. What
if we flipped a lot of the things?
Local-first is all about data. And like
any sort of like applications, there's
things you can switch out more easily.
Maybe you switch out like an Apache HTTP
server for like an Engine X HTTP server,
etc. Like that that's like relatively
easy to do. But when it comes to like
radically changing the data architecture
of the application, it might still be
easy enough to switch from my sequel to
Postgres. But when you really change
like where does data live, where does it
created, how does it flow, etc. That
suddenly becomes one of the hardest
things you can do when you build an
application. Even today with AI and like
genetic engineering, etc. That's still
like one of the hardest things to
change. And I think one of the highest
leverage ways as a software architect,
you can influence the foundations for an
application whether it feels good or
whether it feels terrible and in many
ways.
Local first is just like a radical
departure from like the at least the
status quo of typical web apps. In a
way, it's also like back to the future
to like where things started in a way
since like most computers back then were
un-networked. So like by definition,
everything had to be on that computer.
And then step-by-step with the internet,
we've shifted that into the cloud and
like this is where like all apps
were like thin shells that only
communicated with a fat server. But I
think local first wanted to see like
hey, can we have the best of both
worlds? Can we have the connectivity of
cloud software where it's like always
available, where I can maybe like buy a
new computer, log into everything and
everything is still there. That's not a
big deal.
But also where we can have really high
expectations for the applications that
they work in any circumstances. It's
also that I don't lose my data. I'm sure
like Martin and Adam, etc. They have
like uh a great job of like motivating
the ideals of local first. But for me,
it's like all about like really the
quality of software, like pursuing the
highest quality of software. But like
that's never done in a vacuum. That's
always
relative to what the certain application
is. Like if you're building Google Maps,
you have very different trade-offs
compared to if you're building Airbnb.
But uh there's like for Google Maps,
like being offline in a place where
you've maybe pre-cached is like a very
important thing. Whereas like for
Airbnb, like other trade-offs might be
very important. So I think it's always
important to think through which sort of
trade-offs can you apply for the kind of
application that you want to build.
>> Okay, so you you did a a great job of uh
hiding the it depends between other
other parts because that's what you I
heard you say. It all depends on what
you want to build and then based on that
decide on your trade-offs and uh just
make sure that you have everything that
it takes.
And I'm very happy that you didn't say
it because as a guild of uh engineers,
we have a tendency of always be hiding
behind it depends. So
>> [laughter]
>> you didn't build neither
uh clone of Airbnb, you didn't build a
clone of Google Maps, but you built an
audio application or a music application
if I got it right.
>> Yeah, that's right. Uh I mean, this is
another big passion of mine for for a
long time is is music. Uh I used to be a
DJ in the past as well and we can see
that progression of software like
playing out there. I started like
building a music library with like vinyl
records, but also when I'm back in the
days, etc. And that was like really like
an important part of like who I was,
like a big hobby. And so I was proud to
have like a music collection. Then over
time, we got things like Spotify and
YouTube, etc. And like that gave us like
I still use it on a daily basis, gives

see can a better client layer on top of

a very long time. And when I then
through Peter and Adam heard about the
ideas of local-first, this is where it
clicked for me and I felt okay, I can
actually now like try to build this. So,
local-first was sort of like the
catalyst for me to be bold enough to try
to build this. So, sort of like a
third-party client for wherever music
lives in the same way as how you can use
superhuman for example with your Gmail
account.
But then in order for me to build this,
this was like I I started on on that in
2020, Automerge was like very very early
on and as it all depends how you
architect that data, there was like one
thing I felt like in particular strong
about with sort of a technological
trauma from Prisma if you want, which is

how does data like move around, like
where is it stored, but also how does
your database schema and your data
model, how does it evolve over time? And
I felt very compelled by like one
particular idea or like technical
architecture, which is event sourcing. I

like explored more like on server side,
maybe in the financial space, but I also
saw a ton of potential to apply it

like technologies, for example, Redux

I feel like this idea was still not
pushed far enough. And this is where I

unlock the ideals of local first instead

event sourcing on this? And this is

and yang, as I started building the

Riffle. Nicolas and Jeffrey both

like SQLite-based and

an open-source project anyone can use.

app. What are the trade-offs you can

Local First FM podcast, we also did an

local first landscape which we can maybe
link to. This gives you a nice overview
of like, at least back then, all the
different local first technologies out
there trying to compare them across like
many different dimensions, etc.
>> Yep. That was definitely a technology
soup. It felt like
very very healthy.
>> Yeah, I think the domain here of like a
music app, etc. me like being a DJ as a

motivation. But I think the more
important part is this idea of an app

think about a few technological

step forward. For example, if you think
about
Google Docs or Figma or Linear. Like all

Whether for Google Docs that you saw
someone else's cursor and you could

a canvas where you could collaborate and

data architecture compared to like what
your typical JavaScript web app was

last remaining frontier that we need to

Sort of like a meta schema layer that's

not by the developer. And in order to

This is where I felt event sourcing was

and then combined with SQLite as a view

So, the app can in real time query all
the data. Those were kind of like the
two key parts of innovation. One is like
making SQLite reactive and fast enough
that it can actually run in the same
thread where your front-end web app

sourcing and bring that together. This

stack all all over the a given period,

and you want to just start tagging and

>> Exactly. And another key part of this is

different sources. This is where it

Linear where like each Linear issue you

an incredible set of like external data
sources that can also like change in

like Spotify might remove something from

still want to have sort of like a
tombstone of a track where all the tags

maybe if I have the same track available
from another source where it's still
there, that's like deduplicated, etc.
And like this makes it a very important
aspect of like how can you keep that
data sane over time? This where it was
where event sourcing was like a great
foundation compared to to CRDTs where
you can also like make changes to your
application logic and then just like
replay throughout the entire like
history instead of like mutating an
object. But this gets kind of like now
rabbit hole into the ideas of like Live
Store and event sourcing. But if we're
talking about local first, it is more
important that I just wanted to provide
the best possible user experience to
users who what is important to them is
like they use Overtone to curate their
own music library. And like the worst
thing that could happen there is like
that their data is gone or that data is
like wrong in some way or data is lost.
It's corrupted. This was for me like the
highest order bid basically.
Additionally to like unlocking the best
possible user experience where the app
feels as fast as like a triple A game.
>> That means that the app itself is
a web app which is very very fast on the
local machine, but it has a centralized
place where the data is actually saved.
So, if something happens, you do have a
place where the data will come back.
It's not stored on your machine and when
your machine is dying, right?
>> It's both. So, in this particular case,
it has like a couple of different origin
points. Obviously, whether my app exists
or not, some data lives in Spotify or
like Spotify drops it at some point.
That's something I need to integrate
with. But like in the app locally, all
of like the enrichments happens locally
and it's just synced into a sync back
end that in case I use like use this on
a different machine or on a phone, etc.,
it gets synced. But like all of the data
that actually has the source of truth in
live store, the source of truth has been
the client. It's just that now a sync
server helps facilitate to propagate and
back up that data. In that that regard,
you basically get the best of both
worlds where you have a client that
never has to like reload some data if it
already has seen something, but if you
for example need to set up a new
computer, you can resync everything you
want and you get real-time collaboration
as well.
>> That's nice.
Okay, so just to make sure that I got
it. Whenever you make a change on your
local machine, an event is generated and
then it's stored locally and then
probably propagated through a sync
server somewhere on the web and also the
other way around if somebody else is
using another instance or whatever, you
have it on your phone.
You do something on your phone, it's
going the same route and then everything
is is synchronized.
>> That's right. The way how it works is
very similar to how Git works. In that
regard, that you have sort of like a
push-pull model, and with Git typically,
if you try to push something, and the
server's already had, you need to like
pull first, rebase, or you need to force
push. Live Store works in a very similar
way. But, fundamentally, this is where I
think Martin is probably like the data
godfather in that regard about
distributed systems and so on.
Fundamentally, we're dealing with
distributed systems here, and we need to
like figure out like some trade-offs
somehow, and CRDTs figured them out in
some way. Event Sourcing takes a
different path. Fundamentally, it's like
very similar ideas, just differently
exposed. Martin has given a great talk
at some point about turning the database
inside out, which is what is Event
Sourcing.
And this is the path I've been taking.
But, besides like CRDTs and Event
Sourcing, there's also like different
approaches that folks explore in the
local-first world and and syncing world,
where it's more about like having an
authoritative centralized database
that's a bit more traditional to like
your typical like Ruby on Rails stack,

have a sync engine based on queries that

down the data that is the result for

of like a always-up-to-date smart
caching layer. That's like another
approach that's been taken by by a
couple of really interesting
technologies with like Zero or Electric
SQL parsing etc.
>> Okay. Great.
Now, let's say that
you share your experience.
You have the experience of building
Prisma, and what you took from that, you
used
while putting together Overtone,
plus building the Live Store together
with your friends.
But now
you have the two two options.
What would you advise somebody with that
wants to embrace local first for their
apps?
And what would be maybe the limitations
that there are still available?
>> I think the first question that someone
needs to figure out is should they
really build their app in a local first
way or not? Local first is not just
better and like in the past you've built
this in sort of like a more
cloud-centric way and now local first is
here and now it clearly you should build
local first. That's not the case.
Building apps in local first way comes
at a cost in multiple ways. You need to
think harder about your data
architecture. You need to think more
about like where does data need to be
available and which way, how will it
grow? For example, when Uber started out
maybe in some cities, the database was
much smaller than when they rolled out
to all the cities across the world where
the database is much larger. This is
where they needed to like rethink their
data architecture all the time, but it
was easier because data architecture was
just a back-end concern and not really
like a concern for the client. With
local first, you're like making the
client a much more fundamental aspect of
like the data architecture from the
start. And if something grows in a much
more unbounded way, that really needs to
be taken into consideration. So with
local first, you need to think much more
about how can you slice and dice and
break down different parts of your data
model, of your data layer. You just need
to think a lot more up front about that
and then see is that feasible, is it
worth it? And only if you think that the
user experience that you want to unlock
with that kind of like how important are
those ideals of local first software for
your particular app? If they're very
important, then go for it. And then step
number two is kind of figure out the
right data architecture. And from the
right data architecture, figure out the
the right technology, whether you want
to use something
when you want to use CRDTs, like
exploring AutoMerge, exploring Yjs,
Loro, etc. If you want to use a
different architecture, maybe explore
LiveStore or other technologies. But I
would really not skip the first step.
It's like, is local first the right
thing for you to begin with or not? You
should find the reason why you shouldn't
do it basically. And only if you've said
not no, I still want it. It's still like
worth it for us, then continue. Since
it's it's not like a decision of like
oh, which web router am I using that you
can much more easily like change later.
This is going to be probably the most
fundamental decision you make about your
application.
>> Do you have a quiz or decision tree?
Like, okay, do you want to use local
first? Yes. And then other questions
that there are people should should
respond to.
What questions would you ask yourself?
>> So, how important is it that your
application
works offline? This one. And like, you
can also think about it synonymously.

important is it that your app works

how important is it for end users to own

like how we can best build and model
your your app and architecture in a
